title: Foundations of Portfolio Theory — Nobel lecture
why: An author’s retrospective on how diversification and portfolio choice became a quantitative framework. It provides historical context for the mathematics rather than a trading recipe.
prerequisites: Expected value, variance, covariance, constrained optimization.
readFor: Identify the distinction between choosing securities individually and choosing their combined distribution. Connect the discussion to wᵀΣw and the efficient frontier.
limits: Lecture and PDF were identified through the official Nobel source; direct fetching was restricted during this audit. This is a 1990 lecture, not the original 1952 article. Historical theory does not resolve noisy expected-return estimates.
exercise: Construct two equal-weight assets with identical volatility. Vary correlation and plot portfolio volatility; explain what changes and what remains assumed.

title: The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities
why: Foundational primary research on consistent option valuation through hedging and no-arbitrage reasoning.
prerequisites: Calculus, discounting, probability, a one-step binomial replication.
readFor: Read the pricing argument before the final formula. List every market and price-process assumption needed for replication, then relate delta to the hedge.
limits: Publisher abstract verified; full text may require institutional or paid access. Do not purchase automatically. Idealized continuous hedging is not a guarantee under jumps, costs or discrete trading.
exercise: Replicate a call in a two-state model, then add a transaction cost and explain which exact-arbitrage argument becomes imperfect.

title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting
authors: David H. Bailey, Jonathan M. Borwein, Marcos López de Prado and Qiji Jim Zhu
why: Studies how selecting a historical winner can produce poor subsequent ranking; useful for understanding research selection rather than only final performance.
prerequisites: Train/validation separation, rank statistics, multiple testing.
readFor: Trace how candidate strategies are compared across partitions and how in-sample selection is related to out-of-sample ranking. Distinguish the diagnostic from a universal probability of live failure.
limits: Author preprint is openly accessible; journal publication is 2017 and preprint dates differ. Partitioning and dependence assumptions must be assessed for your data. It does not repair look-ahead leakage or bad fills.
exercise: Generate null return series for many candidates. Compare the selected winner with an unselected candidate on a fresh period and report the full candidate count.

title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality
authors: David H. Bailey and Marcos López de Prado
why: A primary treatment of why a selected Sharpe ratio needs adjustment for search and distributional characteristics.
prerequisites: Sharpe ratio, sampling variation, skewness, kurtosis and selection bias.
readFor: Identify the benchmark against which a selected Sharpe is evaluated and the inputs reflecting the search process. Separate observed performance from confidence in an underlying effect.
limits: Author PDF verified. Trial dependence and incomplete search records complicate inputs. A favorable statistic does not establish execution feasibility, causal correctness or future stability.
exercise: Hold observed Sharpe constant while changing sample length and the number of attempted candidates. Explain why the evidence assessment should change.

title: … and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
authors: Campbell R. Harvey, Yan Liu and Heqing Zhu
why: Explains why conventional isolated-test thresholds can be misleading when a field searches hundreds of candidate return factors.
prerequisites: Hypothesis testing, t-statistics, familywise error and false discovery.
readFor: Study the link between the number of proposed factors and the evidential hurdle. Note the role of correlated tests and the definition of the research family.
limits: 2014 working paper; published in 2016. Its proposed thresholds are model-dependent, not a universal rule that a t-statistic above three proves an edge. Different papers debate false-discovery estimates.
exercise: Document every variation in a small research sweep. Compare unadjusted significance with a clearly stated multiple-testing correction and discuss dependence.

title: Time Series Momentum
authors: Tobias J. Moskowitz, Yao Hua Ooi and Lasse H. Pedersen
why: An empirical primary paper distinguishing an instrument’s own return history from ranking assets against each other.
prerequisites: Excess returns, futures, volatility scaling and time-series evaluation.
readFor: Extract the universe, lookback, holding period, scaling and evaluation choices before attempting a reproduction. State precisely how time-series and cross-sectional momentum differ.
limits: Authors’ research page verified. Its historical multi-asset evidence is not evidence for an Indian intraday single-stock strategy. Costs, data access and contract rolling require separate implementation.
exercise: Write a one-page replication specification. Mark each unavailable dataset or assumption before writing code, and compare against a zero-signal baseline.

title: Momentum Crashes
authors: Kent Daniel and Tobias J. Moskowitz
why: A companion failure-mode reading: average strategy returns can hide concentrated losses in particular market environments.
prerequisites: Momentum construction, drawdown, conditional risk and regression.
readFor: Inspect the definition of momentum, the periods of extreme loss and the proposed connection between market conditions and strategy exposure.
limits: NBER search metadata verified; direct page fetching returned 403 during this audit. 2014 working-paper version. Historical crash descriptions do not make future regime labels observable in advance.
exercise: Compare a strategy’s unconditional mean with outcomes in a predeclared stress subset. Then build a causal state estimate and explain why it differs from hindsight classification.

title: Expected Shortfall and Beyond
why: A primary mathematical discussion of tail-risk measures and how portfolio risk can be attributed to components.
prerequisites: Quantiles, distributions, expectation and portfolio dependence.
readFor: Understand why a quantile alone leaves tail severity undescribed. Study coherence and the interpretation of risk contributions, keeping sign conventions explicit.
limits: Open author preprint verified. Mathematical properties depend on precise definitions; estimating rare tails from short market samples remains difficult. A coherent risk measure is not an accurate forecast by itself.
exercise: Construct two loss distributions with the same chosen VaR but different tail losses. Calculate their expected shortfall and explain the practical distinction.
